Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2017: Seeded and volunteer plant material look very good the first year following the fire. Composition and vigor of seeded species is very impressive. Perennial composition has already reached and exceeded the 5-year 40% composition objective. The 40% composition objective is measured using nested plot frequency of perennial vegetation. Relative frequency of perennial species in 2017 averaged approximately 73% for three monitoring locations.
2018: Three Nested Plot Frequency transects were completed on the West Government Creek ESR on
May 31 and June 14, 2018. Seeded and volunteer plant material continue to look very good into
the second year following the fire. Plant vigor of seeded species is excellent. Perennial
composition once again exceeded the 5-year 40% composition objective. The 40% composition
objective is measured using nested plot frequency of perennial vegetation. Relative frequency of
perennial species in 2018 averaged approximately 70% for three monitoring locations.

2019: Two Nested Plot Frequency transects were completed on the West Government Creek ESR on June 25 and June 29, 2019. Seeded and volunteer plant material continue to look very good into the second year following the fire. Plant vigor of seeded species is excellent. Perennial composition once again exceeded the 5-year 40% composition objective. The 40% composition objective is measured using nested plot frequency of perennial vegetation. Relative frequency of perennial species in 2018 averaged approximately 60% for two monitoring locations. Detailed vegetation monitoring results are documented below.

2020: Three Nested Plot Frequency transects were completed on the West Government Creek ESR on June 17 and June 18, 2020. Seeded and volunteer plant material continue to look vigorous into the fourth year following the fire. Perennial composition once again exceeded the 5-year 40% composition objective. The 40% composition objective is measured using nested plot frequency of perennial vegetation. Relative frequency of perennial species in 2020 was a phenomenal average of 83% for three monitoring locations. Detailed vegetation monitoring results are documented below.

2021: Due to budget restrictions vegetation and weeds monitoring was not conducted during the 2021 field season. The West Government Creek ESR project has met its objective of 40% relative perennial frequency composition in the first and all subsequent years for monitored sites.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The Lost Fire occurred on the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Northern California District
(NOD), Surprise Field Office (SFO) area. It was one of 7 fires that started on the 5th of August
in NOD by lightning. The fire was located approximately 21 miles east/southeast of the town of
Eagleville, CA. The fire started approximately 1 mile north of the Lost Creek Road near the Los
Angeles Department of Water and Power twin 500 KV power lines. When first reported by a
Nevada Department of Wildlife employee, the fire was estimated between 500 – 800 acres in
size and growing. During the initial time period, the SFO Surprise Valley Fire Station was
fighting several new lightning fires. Initial attack suppression forces were dispatched by the
Susanville Interagency Dispatch Center and Jerry Wheeler DC-3206 assumed the role as Lost
Incident Commander. Around the time of ignition, surface winds increased from the southwest
and ranged from 5 to 8 mph with gusts up to 15 mph. On August 5th, a ridge of high pressure
over the Four Corners region intensified while a thermal trough developed over central Nevada.
The combination of these two climatic features increased heating and resulted in the
development of an extremely dry air mass over the fire area. High temperatures were 5 to 8
degrees above normal and ranged from 92 to 97 degrees. Corresponding minimum relative
humidity (RH) values dropped to 5-9 percent. The lowest RH recorded during the fire was 2
percent. On August 5th, the fire exceeded the capabilities of initial response efforts and the fire
burned through the evening and was estimated to be approximately 9,000 acres by the morning
of August 6th. During the afternoon and evening of August 6th and 7th, the fire made significant
runs to the east and northeast, consuming approximately 15,000 acres each day. On August 8th,
the fire spread primarily northeast and southeast following fuels and terrain for another 15,000
acres. Suppression actions and a major change in fuel type reduced fire spread on August 9th, but
the fire area still increased in size by approximately 3,900 acres. The fire was contained on
August 12th at approximately 61,537 acres.

Objectives: Stabilize soils and limit erosion on upper elevation steep slopes within the burn area to reduce erosion from wind and to re-establish important habitat for mule deer and other wildlife species.
Planned_Implementation: During implementation we had excellent moisture with snow covered ground with good even distribution of seeded species. Winds did not exceed 3-5 MPH during implementation.
Actual_Implementation: We found seeded species (predominately small burnet and forage kochia) to be widely spaced (2 -10 meters) but evenly distributed across all the areas traveled through in route to our randomly selected monitoring sites.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
We found seeded species (predominately small burnet and forage kochia)
to be widely spaced (2 -10 meters) but evenly distributed across all the areas traveled through in route to
our randomly selected monitoring sites. Only density was read the initial year. Using the USGS monitoring
methodology (Modified from: Monitoring Manuel for Grasses, Shrublands and Savannah Ecosystems,
Herrick et al 2005.) being recommended for ESR, the average for each site was the following: Site 1=0.4
rooted plants/m\xb2. Although this falls below our original objective: 3 rooted plants/m\xb2, I believe our
objective was too high for this project in that our goal was to stabilize exposed soils in addition to reestablishing
and/or improving forage for wildlife, not to create a vegetation community structure stand
change. Given the degree of natural recovery of surviving grasses, the establishment of small burnet and
forage kochia (forage) and Wyoming Big sagebrush seedlings(Sage grouse crucial habitat) observed on
much of the project (but not showing up in transects), we concluded this first year was partially successful
in achieving our goals if not our objectives. We further believe this seeding will enhance and quicken the
recovery of this burned area.

Hayden allotments for 2 years or until monitoring stabilization objectives are met.

o Conduct 25 acres of noxious weed inventory and treat noxious weeds with BLM
approved herbicides, as necessary.

3,604 acres of public lands and was contained on July 21st, 2007. The Barrel Springs Fire burned important Mule Deer winter range.

Hayden allotments for 2 years or until monitoring stabilization objectives are met.

Anatone bluebunch wheatgrass, Idaho fescue and Basin big sage were seeded to add vegetation structure and species richness to the treatment areas.\r\nEstablish three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Provide cover and forage for wildlife and BLM Special Status Species/migratory birds, including crucial winter habitat for mule deer, and sage grouse habitat.
Planned_Implementation:
Aerially seed approximately 1,929 acres with a low elevation wildlife mixture of Idaho Fescue, “Anatone” Bluebunch Wheatgrass, and Wyoming Big Sagebrush.  

•	Lower elevation on 1,570 acres.  The seed mix is Wyoming big sagebrush, basin big sagebrush Bannock cultivar), thickspike wheatgrass and Western yarrow.

Acres treated will be seeded aerially based on ecological site potentials with the use of a helicopter with a seed broadcast bucket.  Seeding in swaths (e.g. seed application on 80 foot swath, leave 160 foot swath and apply again) that allow for plant establishment and future seed sources will be prioritized on any “large” areas that burned completely.  Selective spot seeding will also be considered due to the mosaic of vegetation types affected and to avoid intact unburned areas to where specific sagebrush species will be seeded considering site potential.  Acreage would be duplicated on those areas where aerial seeding and on-ground antelope bitterbrush seeding occurs on the same affected site.  Bluebunch wheatgrass might be substituted with Snake River wheatgrass, a native perennial species.

Seed mixtures shown in this subsection would allow for additional rehabilitation of wildlife habitat as well as allow watershed protection and reduce erosion potential.  The consideration of acreage seeded includes, 1) two-tracks for potential vegetated fuel breaks separate from this DNA, 2) private lands and 3) the estimated unburned areas within the perimeter. The seeding would provide cover and forage for at least 250 wildlife species that inhabit sagebrush habitats and interspersed riparian/meadow habitat including sage grouse and mule deer, migratory birds and Special Status Species.  It would also provide vegetation needed for ecological site dynamics.

No data was collected about signs of erosion present on site.

2021: Species richness was moderately high for each plot. Perennials out-number annuals.

Objectives: The primary objective of the treatment is to seed watershed areas of the burn that are at highest risk for significant erosion and non-native species invasion. Watersheds are especially at risk as they generally had the greatest build up of vegetation pre-fire, causing the fire to burn hot and destroy all vegetation and species in the seedbank. \r\nEstablish three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in soil with consideration for site selection factors of soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and potential for seedling establishment.  Protect watershed areas from erosion.
Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed approximately 10062 acres with a watershed protection mixture (\u201cCharleston Watershed Mix\u201d) of \u201cSherman\u201d Big Bluegrass, \u201cBannock\u201d Thickspike Wheatgrass, \u201cSecar\u201d Snake River Wheatgrass, and \u201cMagnar\u201d Basin Wildrye.\r\n\r\nAdd Western Yarrow and Basin Big Sagebrush to the watershed protection seed mixture (\u201cCharleston watershed mix\u201d) of native grasses.
Actual_Implementation:
Due to the availability of water and other resources necessary for regrowth, a mix of both native and non-native species (Snake River wheatgrass, Sherman big bluegrass, Magnar and trailhead Basin wild rye, Bluebunch wheatgrass, Siberian wheatgrass, Idaho Fescue, and Schwendimar and Bannock thickspike wheatgrass) was selected. Additional shrubs were added to the mix, and are discussed in the Burned Area Rehabilitation treatment monitoring section.

Implementation Monitoring:  
The aerial watershed protection seeding was completed during January via fixed wing through an aircraft rental agreement. The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector.  AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure the correct species seed mixture was dispersed over the targeted area at the specified rate. The project inspector ensured treatment met contract specifications.

BAR addition of western yarrow and sagebrush:
“Delar” Small Burnet may have been substituted for Western Yarrow at some indeterminate locations. 
Because implementation was done concurrently with the aerial watershed protection seeding applied under emergency stabilization, only seed costs are reflected here.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Charleston Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding was monitored at seven separate locations (CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, CHWS – 03, CHWS – 04, CHWS – 05, CHWS – 06, CHWS – 07) specifically established to monitor this treatment on all range grazing allotments affected by the fire. 

Monitoring Results: 
2007 – Total seeded species density exceeded the objective density of three plants per square meter at all monitoring locations.  Thickspike Wheatgrass typically made the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  Basin Wildrye was also very successful
2008 – Total seeded species density continued to exceed the objective density of three plants per square meter at CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, CHWS – 03, and CHWS – 05, appearing to increase slightly at CHWS – 01 CHWS – 02, and CHWS – 03.  Total seeded species density appeared to decline at CHWS – 04, CHWS – 05, CHWS – 05, and CHWS – 07.  Thickspike Wheatgrass continued to make the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  All other seeded species declined dramatically and were not recorded, except at CHWS – 04, where Basin Wildrye was recorded at moderate density.  Downward trend in seeded species at CHWS – 04 and CHWS – 05 appears unrelated to competition from native release Sandberg’s Bluegrass: at these monitoring locations Sandberg’s Bluegrass density varied from very high to low-moderate. 
The apparent disappearance of the majority of the seeded species of grasses during the second year of monitoring is problematic, and may be the result of a variety of causes.  Different technicians read the plots at different times of year between 2007 and 2008.  Seedlings may have become established the first year that later died off or went dormant because of persistent drought.  “Quadrat drift” along the paced transects used to monitor this treatment may also have played a role: density fluctuations should be evaluated cautiously.  Disappearance of most seeded species of grasses from the monitoring record the second year may not actually reflect their loss.  Data collected during the third monitoring year may help clarify these problems. 
2009 – Thickspike Wheatgrass density at CHWS – 01 exceeded the target density by nearly four times.  Thickspike Wheatgrass density at CHWS – 02 exceeded the target density by nearly five times.  Total seeded species density for CHWS – 03 approaches the target density, with Thickspike wheatgrass making the greatest contribution.  Thickspike Wheatgrass density for CHWS – 04 exceeds the target density by almost five times.  At CHWS – 05, only one specimen of Snake River Wheatgrass was recorded, other seeded species were not recorded.  At CHWS – 06, Thickspike Wheatgrass exceeded the target density.  At CHWS – 07 Basin Wildrye achieved a density of one and one-half plant per square meter during the final year: other seeded species were not recorded.  Abundant spring rains in later May and early June apparently benefited the establishment and success of this treatment with the monitoring period.  Thickspike Wheatgrass typically made the greatest contribution to seeded species density, exceeding the target density of three plants per square meter by four to five times at CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, and CHWS – 04.  The other seeded grass species appeared to return during the final year of monitoring, suggesting that their absence during 2008 only reflected dormancy and not extirpation.  Many previously unrecorded species appeared in the native release at monitoring sites across the treatment, also reflecting the abundant later spring precipitation.  “On average,” considering the extremely high densities recorded for Thickspike Wheatgrass at many of the monitoring locations and how well established many seeded species appear to be across the treatment, the Charleston Aerial watershed Protection Seeding should be considered fully successful. 

BAR addition:
2007 – Total seeded species density exceeded the objective density of three plants per square meter at all monitoring locations.  Thickspike Wheatgrass typically made the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  
2008 – Total seeded species density continued to exceed the objective density of three plants per square meter at CHWS – 01, CHWS – 02, and CHWS – 03, appearing to increase slightly at CHWS – 01 and CHWS – 02, and appearing to decline slightly at CHWS – 03.  Thickspike Wheatgrass continued to make the greatest contribution to total seeded species density.  
Minor density fluctuations should be evaluated cautiously: they may result from non-repeatability of individual quadrats along a paced transect.  At CHWS – 04 and CHWS – 05 total seeded species densities appeared to undergo steep declines.  Causes of opposite fluctuations in seeded densities between monitoring locations are unknown.  Downward trend in seeded species at CHWS – 04 and CHWS – 05 appears unrelated to competition from native release Sandberg’s Bluegrass: at these monitoring locations Sandberg’s Bluegrass density varied from very high to low-moderate. 
2009 – Small Burnet went unrecorded during the final monitoring year.  It’s presence in the seed mixture was not uniform, and lack of record for the presence of the species the final year may be the result of “quadrat drift” along the paced transects used to monitor this treatment.  Basin Big Sagebrush appeared to be well established at low to moderate densities at most monitoring locations by the close of the monitoring period.  Western Yarrow exceeded the objective density at CHWS – 03, but the species was “double seeded” at this location (as discussed in the analysis of the treatment above.)  At other locations Western Yarrow appeared well-established at low to moderate densities by the final year.  Basin Big Sagebrush and Western Yarrow were both recorded at low density at CHWS – 05. Basin Big Sagebrush was recorded at very low density and Western Yarrow was not recorded at CHWS – 07.  Results varied at the  numerous monitoring locations, but we may consider the addition of sagebrush and yarrow to the Charleston Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding partially successful. 
Regarding native release, reasons for the apparent precipitous decline in Sandberg’s Bluegrass density at CHWS – 03 from 2008 to 2009 are not known, but may reflect non-repeatability of individual quadrats along the paced transect.  Many previously unrecorded species were encountered at CHWS – 03 during 2009: they may have out-competed the Sandberg’s Bluegrass.  Alternately, the Prairie Junegrass and Kentucky Bluegrass identified during 2009 may have been previously misidentified as Sandberg’s Bluegrass.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Implementation of the proposed action described in the Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation Plan DNA for the Charleston Complex will protect soils in the burned area, including preventing potential loss of soil due to wind and water erosion&* will reduce potential invasion and establishment of noxious weeds and cheatgrass&* will provide quality forage for livestock and wildlife&* and will facilitate meeting established standards and guidelines for livestock grazing.  

Exclusion of livestock grazing is necessary to allow seedling establishment, restore plant vigor and seed production, and to allow reestablishment of preferred species and to deter invasion of undesirable species.  The proposed fence will be constructed around the burn perimeter to keep grazing animals off the recovering burn to allow establishment of seeded and pre-fire vegetation species.  This temporary fencing will be used in conjunction with existing fences to protect the burn area from grazing.  This fencing and subsequent rest from grazing will allow for plants to re-establish and develop effective root depths and root reserves.  Vegetation establishment will help reduce the risk of dust and ash storms decreasing visibility on Interstate 80.  Vegetation establishment will help reduce the risk of accelerated soil erosion and mud flows into Mary&$s River and other areas of concern and provide for soil stabilization.  Vegetation associated with wetlands, riparian zones, and floodplains will be allowed to reestablish. 

The broadcast seedings within drainages and low lying areas and aerial seeding on slopes will provide for soil stabilization and will reduce the potential invasion of cheatgrass, and any other nonnative noxious weeds.  The seedings will also provide cover and forage for area wildlife populations and nesting habitat for migratory birds.  Successful seeding of some drainages and the low lying areas near the South Fork of the Humboldt River and its tributaries will help reduce runoff and trap sediment, which will help prevent further degradation to the water quality.  Successful seeding of the drainages and low lying areas will also help protect aquatic species habitat from receiving excessive amounts of sediment and provide for streambank stabilization.

Control of noxious weeds is consistent with the management plans for the resource and will help protect the ecological integrity, biodiversity, and site productivity of this shrub-steppe plant community.  Treatment of noxious weeds is necessary to comply with Nevada State Laws, to implement the Integrated Weed Management Program of the Elko Field Office, and to be responsible neighbors to the adjacent private landowners.  Working cooperatively with local weed management groups and private landowners will achieve better weed management.

The proposed action conforms to the 1985 Wells Resource Management Plan (RMP), as it was amended for fire management on September 29, 2004.  The decision for fire rehabilitation from the Approved Fire Management Amendment, page 20, is to “Conduct fire rehabilitation activities to emulate historic or pre-fire ecosystem structure, functioning, diversity and/or to restore a healthy stable ecosystem.”  The proposed action is consistent with resource objectives of the plan and with other Federal, state, local and tribal laws, regulations, policies and plans to the maximum extent possible.

The high elevation areas treated with this mix are especially susceptible to permanent habitat conversion as they do not respond well to fire and are slow to reestablish.
Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed approximately 4296 acres with a high elevation wildlife mix of Western Yarrow and Mountain Big Sagebrush.\r\n\r\nThis plan calls for EVERY THIRD SWATH seeding over 14,976 acres FOR A TOTAL OF 4992 ACRES.  All public lands.
Actual_Implementation: Sagebrush and yarrow were seeded to add vegetation structure and species richness to treated areas.  \r\nThe aerial wildlife seeding was completed in January via fixed wing through an aircraft rental agreement. The ground crew consisted of BLM helitack and a project inspector. AG Nav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file.  Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure the correct seed mixture was dispersed over the target area at the specified rate.  A project inspector was present to ensure treatment met contract specifications.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

The Charleston Aerial Wildlife (High Elevation) Seeding was monitored at three separate locations. One was specifically established to monitor this treatment (CHWH – 01), one was established to monitor the Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding where it is overlapped by the Aerial Wildlife (High Elevation) Seeding (CHWS – 03), and one was established to monitor native release on a Mountain Ridge range site within the high elevation wildlife seeding (CHNR – 05). 

Monitoring Results: 
2007 – At CHWH – 01, Western Yarrow was present at a density near one and three-quarters plants square meter (exceeding the objective density of one plant per square meter), Mountain Big Sagebrush was recorded at a density approaching one-half plant per square meter.  At CHWS – 03, Western Yarrow appeared to increase to a density approaching three plants per square meter (well exceeding the objective density of one plant per square meter), Mountain Big Sagebrush was present at a density near one-third plant per square meter.  At CHNR – 05 neither Western Yarrow nor Mountain Big Sagebrush were recorded. 
2008 – At CHWH – 01, Western Yarrow appeared to decline in density by more than one plant per square meter, Mountain Big Sagebrush was not recorded.  At CHWS – 03, Western Yarrow maintained a density near two and one-half plants per square meter but Mountain Big Sagebrush was not recorded.  Fluctuations should be evaluated cautiously because individual quadrat frames are not absolutely repeatable from year to year along a paced transect.  At CHNR – 05 Western Yarrow was not recorded but Mountain Big Sagebrush approached a density of one-half plant per square meter. 
2009 – Monitoring plot CHNR – 05  was specifically established to monitor native release at the request of the Elko range staff and only monitored ESR treatments incidentally.  It was not re-read by ESR staff during the final year of monitoring.  
Western Yarrow exceeded the objective density of three plants per square meter at CHWS – 03 during the final year of monitoring.  Western Yarrow was observed in abundance in the areas surrounding CHWS – 03, visible in parallel whitish “stripes” across the upland landscape that indicated flight paths.  Since Western Yarrow was “double seeded” at the CHWS – 03 monitoring location (that is, seeded with both the Aerial Wildlife (high elevation) Seeding and the Aerial Watershed Protection Seeding that overlapped there,) an exact determination of which treatment provided the yarrow that was recorded cannot be made.  However, evidence of both seedings was clear where a slightly broader whitish stripe ran diagonally to the upland parallel stripes, down the middle of the V-shaped intermittent drainage seeded during the watershed protection treatment.  Western Yarrow was recorded at a moderate density exceeding one-third plant per square meter at CHWH – 01; Mountain Big Sagebrush was not recorded.  Success varied between monitoring locations and throughout the monitoring period.  The Charleston Aerial Wildlife (high elevation) Seeding may be considered partially successful based upon solely upon observations and recorded density for Western Yarrow at CHWS – 03. Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Implementation of the proposed action described in the Emergency Stabilization and Rehabilitation Plan DNA for the Charleston Complex will protect soils in the burned area, including preventing potential loss of soil due to wind and water erosion&* will reduce potential invasion and establishment of noxious weeds and cheatgrass&* will provide quality forage for livestock and wildlife&* and will facilitate meeting established standards and guidelines for livestock grazing.  

Exclusion of livestock grazing is necessary to allow seedling establishment, restore plant vigor and seed production, and to allow reestablishment of preferred species and to deter invasion of undesirable species.  The proposed fence will be constructed around the burn perimeter to keep grazing animals off the recovering burn to allow establishment of seeded and pre-fire vegetation species.  This temporary fencing will be used in conjunction with existing fences to protect the burn area from grazing.  This fencing and subsequent rest from grazing will allow for plants to re-establish and develop effective root depths and root reserves.  Vegetation establishment will help reduce the risk of dust and ash storms decreasing visibility on Interstate 80.  Vegetation establishment will help reduce the risk of accelerated soil erosion and mud flows into Mary&$s River and other areas of concern and provide for soil stabilization.  Vegetation associated with wetlands, riparian zones, and floodplains will be allowed to reestablish. 

The broadcast seedings within drainages and low lying areas and aerial seeding on slopes will provide for soil stabilization and will reduce the potential invasion of cheatgrass, and any other nonnative noxious weeds.  The seedings will also provide cover and forage for area wildlife populations and nesting habitat for migratory birds.  Successful seeding of some drainages and the low lying areas near the South Fork of the Humboldt River and its tributaries will help reduce runoff and trap sediment, which will help prevent further degradation to the water quality.  Successful seeding of the drainages and low lying areas will also help protect aquatic species habitat from receiving excessive amounts of sediment and provide for streambank stabilization.

Control of noxious weeds is consistent with the management plans for the resource and will help protect the ecological integrity, biodiversity, and site productivity of this shrub-steppe plant community.  Treatment of noxious weeds is necessary to comply with Nevada State Laws, to implement the Integrated Weed Management Program of the Elko Field Office, and to be responsible neighbors to the adjacent private landowners.  Working cooperatively with local weed management groups and private landowners will achieve better weed management.

The proposed action conforms to the 1985 Wells Resource Management Plan (RMP), as it was amended for fire management on September 29, 2004.  The decision for fire rehabilitation from the Approved Fire Management Amendment, page 20, is to “Conduct fire rehabilitation activities to emulate historic or pre-fire ecosystem structure, functioning, diversity and/or to restore a healthy stable ecosystem.”  The proposed action is consistent with resource objectives of the plan and with other Federal, state, local and tribal laws, regulations, policies and plans to the maximum extent possible.

Actual_Implementation: A handful of sites were reviewed by an Interdisciplinary Team to evaluate reintroduction of grazing to those select pastures. Four areas have been identified as needing treatment in the form of herbicide control for cheatgrass and seeding the appropriate seed mix for the site.  These sites will be monitored as seeding treatments following treatment.  Erosion is an issue at some sites, but appears to be minimizing.  Further monitoring is needed to determine if a trend towards natural recovery is being made.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: Effectiveness monitoring will include visits to the site by range staff and other BLM employees to ensure that there is no livestock within the burned area and that no unauthorized use has taken place.

Objectives: For entire contract area: Hand plant 375,000 seedlings in the Jarbidge and Burley Field Office area of the Twin Falls District BLM.
Planned_Implementation:
For entire contract area: Hand plant 375,000 seedlings in the Jarbidge and Burley Field Office area of the Twin Falls District BLM. 

2.1 SEEDLING PREPARATION
A. The Contractor shall be responsible for removal of seedlings from the packaging prior to planting.
B. The Contractor will be required to consolidate and organize all packaging used to transport seedlings
including containers, plastic wrapping, plastic bags, and boxes.
C. The Contractor will protect products from damage while loading and in transit to project unit(s).
2.2 SITE PREPARATION
A. Preparing the Planting Hole - Planting holes shall be located near the center of the prepared area and shall be
oriented at an angle between perpendicular to the slope and true vertical (see Attachment). Planting holes
must be two inches deeper than the maximum root length of the seedlings.
2.3 PLANTING METHODS
A. The following requirements will apply to all planting units, unless identified otherwise.
B. Proper selection of planting site is important to provide protection from animal damage, sun, wind, loose
debris, and other agents detrimental to seedling survival and growth.
C. Plant spacing will be 8-15 feet and plants will be planted in large groups utilizing a grid pattern by planting
crews. Planting grid patterns must cover the entire planting project unit with exceptions for avoidance areas
(see section H below) or as allowed by the Project Inspector due to site conditions.
D. Plants will be placed no closer than 3 feet away from existing live brush plants, but could be placed closer to
standing dead shrubs.
E. Clearing efforts will be required to prepare the site for planting and maintaining required spacing.
F. An unplantable area (spot) will be indicated by the Project Inspector prior to planting on the project site. The
Project Inspector will make the determination whether a site is plantable or unplantable.
G. Where an unplantable spot is encountered: The planter shall move over the unplantable spot and plant in the
closest plantable spot available, and then resume required spacing. Examples of unplantable spots are:
I. Rock outcrops, talus slopes, and areas of stone, cobbles or gravel or 12" deep.
2. Sites with obvious rodent or insect (ant hills) activity.
3. Sites with obvious run-off, i.e. bottom of drainages.
4. Animal & human travel paths - planting sites shall be a minimum of five feet, each side, from travel
paths.
5. Within .25 miles of livestock troughs or supplement sites.
6. Within 50 feet of two-track roads or fence lines.
7. Within 300 feet of main travel roads.
8. Cultural avoidance areas as identified on the project maps.
H. Planting will not occur on slick spots where they exist, or near other sensitive areas.
Actual_Implementation: This project consisted of the grow and hand planting of 45,000 6 cubic inch containerized Wyoming big sagebrush and 5,000 antelope bitterbrush seedlings over an area of about 4,100 acres. The seedlings were planted to mostly moist ground in patches of 500 to 1,000 plants. See the attached map for the project location.  \r\n\r\nThe grower for the seedlings was awarded in a separate contract (140L2619P0006_2019 TFD Fuels Shrub Grow) to Desert Sage Farm, LLC of Mackay, ID (greenhouse located in Oakley, ID). The Planting contractor was Quicksilver Contracting Company of La Pine, OR. Foremen for the planting crew was Victor Sanchez and Cristian . The crew consisted of 16 planters. The project was completed using hoedads and UTV\u2019s for transporting seedlings. The project was started on October 4, 2019 and completed October 5, 2019

Objectives: Prior to the West Fork Fire, terraces and benches associated with drainage bottoms supported heavy densities of sagebrush and as a result burned intensively.  Without seeding, these areas are highly susceptible to erosion and to invasions by cheatgrass and other exotic weed species.  Broadcast seeding of perennial grass species along terraces and benches will provide for soil stabilization and will reduce chances of invasive weeds becoming established.  Seeded grasses will also aid in sediment trapping and dissipation of flow energies associated with runoff, resulting in improved water quality in downstream areas. In addition, deep rooted perennial grasses will act to stabilize easily erodible terraces. \r\n\r\nThe primary objective of the treatment is to aerially seed areas that are most at risk for long-term irreversible damage due to the effects of the fire.
Planned_Implementation: Watershed Seeding - Aerial seed approximately 2,425 acres with Western yarrow, Bannock thickspike wheatgrass, Snake River Wheatgrass, Magnar Great Basin wildrye, and Sherman big bluegrass.  Seeding will target drainages and tributaries that burned with moderate to high severity.  Basin big sagebrush will also be added to the mix under the Rehabilitation Plan.
Actual_Implementation: A watershed mix of Snake River wheatgrass, Streambank wheatgrass, Idaho fescue, Basin Wildrye, Thickspike wheatgrass, Big bluegrass, Sanfoin and Basin big sagebrush was applied to the fire. \r\nThis treatment was done in December with a helicopter through and aircraft rental agreement. AgNav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file. Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure that seed was being dispersed in the proper area and at the specified rate. A project inspector was present throughout the process to ensure the treatment met contract specifications.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

In the first year post-fire and post-treatment, both seeded and native species were recorded in the study plots on the West Fork Fire. 

On the aerial watershed treatment (WFS3/D-01 and WFS3/D-02), seeded species per square meter were observed with the following density: 
Snake River wheatgrass, .25

Basin wildrye, 13
Big bluegrass, .05

Total seeded species observed per meter: 2.0

The following native release species were also observed within the transects: POSE, SIHY, AGSP, CHVI-8, BASA, PHHO, LUPIN, AMTE, LARE, PHLO and GARA

The following invasive/ potentially invasive species were observed within the transect: BRTE, IVAX, LEPE and DEPI

The goal of reseeding the treatment areas with shrub species is to help provide cover and forage for wildlife; reduce water erosion hazards by stabilizing soils; increase the rate at which native riparian vegetation is restored; maintain a healthy, productive, and diverse plant community; and minimize the establishment of exotic annual plants.  

Emphasis of these rehabilitation seedings have been placed on mule deer, antelope, and sage grouse.  Application of sagebrush seed will target areas that had the existing vegetation community that is being seeded.  

The primary objective of the treatment is to seed areas of the burn that are at high risk for significant erosion and non-native species invasion.
Planned_Implementation: \u2022\tMule Deer Winter Range Seeding \u2013 Aerially seed approximately 11,550 acres with a mix which consists of Mountain big sagebrush, Basin big sagebrush, and Western yarrow.  Treatment emphasis was placed on the most critical areas for mule deer winter range using ecological sites based on vegetation mortality, soil types, precondition vegetation, and consultation with the Nevada Department of Wildlife.
Actual_Implementation: A Mule Deer Winter Range mix of Mountain and Basin big sagebrush and Western Yarrow was applied. \r\nThis treatment was done in December with a helicopter through and aircraft rental agreement. AgNav maps of the aerial seeding were completed for the project file. Aerial seeding was monitored to ensure that seed was being dispersed in the proper area and at the specified rate. A project inspector was present throughout the process to ensure the treatment met contract specifications.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
BLM monitoring personnel assess the seeding areas yearly to evaluate treatment success.  Effectiveness is based on establishment of three seeded plants per square meter rooted firmly in the soil with consideration to site selection factors such as soils, topography, native release of desirable species, and the potential for seedling establishment. Monitoring data is shared with range staff to provide comparisons with unburned reference sites.

In the first year post-fire and post-treatment, both seeded and native species were recorded in the study plots on the West Fork Fire. 

On the Mule deer winter range aerial treatment (WFS3/W-01, WFS3/W-02 and WFS3/W-03) seeded species per square meter were observed with the following density:

Objectives: To prevent accelerated soil erosion, restore canopy cover and ground cover.
Planned_Implementation: Aerial 8,809 acres of burned rangeland. (some areas seeded twice, once with a grass mixture and then with a shrub mixture,\r\ntreatment are at different times of the year.
Actual_Implementation: This is the high elevation mix treatment.  The aerial seeding was done by Thomas Helicopters on 2/11-12/2002. The ground conditions were frozen in the morning thawing in the afternoon with 60-70% snow cover in the higher elevations. The shrub seed was broadcast at high elevations throughout the project and not contour seeded. The grass seed was broadcast in the drainages flying as close as possible for even distribution.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The area is showing good native plant recovery in most areas. The native species pre-fire grasses and forbs have
successfully re-established themselves. The Big Sagebrush seedlings have been established within a portion of the
burned area drainage areas. Observations of sagebrush seedlings were made in portions of the area. The planted
seedling establishment was very favorable in most all of the seeded areas which will provide key forage for many
wildlife species in the area. Soil movement in the steep drainage areas was minimal. Closing pastures and protective
fencing allowed native and seeded species recovery.

The purpose of this project is to reduce the risk of accelerated erosion, restore wildlife habitat, and allow for the recovery of the native vegetation, which burned in the Rough Diamonds fire.  An additional concern was OHV activity in the burned area.

Noxious weeds- Although noxious weeds were not considered a serious problem within this area prior to the burn, small populations of Scotch thistle (Onopordum acanthium), Canada thistle (Cirsium arvense), and white top (Cardaria draba) are known to exist within and near the burned area.

Objectives:
The objective of the weed treatments is to prevent the increase of existing weed populations
and the establishment of additional noxious weed species within the burn area until
desirable vegetation can re-establish. Initial treatment should kill and/or control from
80-90% of targeted weed populations, depending upon the type of weed and/or density of
the infestation. Retreatment by spot spraying on remaining weeds will also be completed
under R5.
Planned_Implementation: Unknown
Actual_Implementation: Treated a total of 10,400 with combination of FY16 acres
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
1. In 2017, mean foliar cover of invasive annual grasses for areas treated with herbicide in the fall of 2015 was
12.52% (Table 8-5). The McBride Creek pasture in the Rockville allotment had the highest invasive annual
grass cover (24.54%). Nearly all of the fall 2015 herbicide application was drill seeded in the fall of 2016. Prefire
these areas likely had relatively high invasive grass annual cover. It appears that the herbicide treatment is
continued to affect annual grass germination into 2017, and the invasive grass cover has remained below 20% in
a majority of the treated area.

In 2017, mean foliar cover of invasive annual grasses for areas treated with herbicide in fall of 2016 was
20.30% (Table 8-6). The Antelope pasture in the Board Corrals allotment had the greatest annual grass cover
(28.31 % ) of all the pastures treated in the fall of 2016. Pre-fire invasive grass cover was likely variable with
cover varying with elevation, aspect, topography and historic land use. Invasive annual grasses in the areas
treated with herbicide in the fall of 2016, had a growing season (plus a fall season) to germinate after the fire
and prior to the first treatment. As per common BLM foliar cover sampling methods, standing dead vegetation
is included in the total foliar cover. For this reason, the foliar cover in 2017 may include some standing dead
vegetation from spring 2016 germination. Although the treatment total for the fall 2016 herbicide treatment
exceeds the maximum stated in the objective, there may still be an opportunity for cover to decrease through
continued suppression of germination and detachment of invasive annual grass stems.

Treatment_Type: Noxious Weeds: Weed Control - Herbicide Application
Objectives: Reduce noxious weeds and prepare seedbed
Planned_Implementation:
Noxious Weed Treatments. Inventory and treat noxious weeds with 458 acres
of aerial and spot treat ground applications best suited to each site and weed
type during the first year. Monitor and re-treat sites if necessary. Identified
noxious weed sites would be treated for two consecutive years.
Actual_Implementation: Aerial Herbicide Application of Telar on 458 acres was completed in October 2021 (FY22) with FY21 funds for the reduction of noxious weeds.\r\nThe proposed seeding areas are the focus of the aerial herbicide treatment of imazapic to prepare the seed bed for aerial seedings focusing on cheatgrass and noxious weed control for seedbed preparation for the aerial seeding treatment to enhance germination and seedling establishment of native perennials.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Treatment effectiveness plots were established during early summer 2022, allowing for monitoring during peak forb growth. The monitoring for summer 2022 will provide a baseline dataset used to describe each treatment overall effectiveness in the subsequent years. Monitoring in 2022 showed, the invasive annual grass cover was 2.2% in the Telar and imazapic aerial herbicide area. The deep-rooted perennial grass for the treated area was slightly over 8%. The shallow-rooted bunchgrasses have a total of 5.6% foliar cover in the treatment area (Table 7-1, 7-2). The Telar and imazapic plots overall had a density of 1.36 plants per m2 (Table 7-1).

Overall, in the two years since the Baldy fire, both herbicide areas are recovering well with little invasive grass or noxious forb presence. The imazapic and Telar treated area showed a high percentage of bare soil 41% (Figure 7-2). These bare soil areas are traditionally thought to be highly susceptible to invasive annual grasses and will be important areas for monitoring in the future.

Monitoring in 2023 showed a drastic increase in invasive grass cover by over 20%, current invasive grass cover is 23.8% (Table 7-2). There was also a good increase in deep-rooted perennial grass cover of 10%. Deep-rooted perennial grass now has a foliar cover of 18.5% within the treatment area. Currently, this area is not meeting any of the treatment objectives but looks like it might meet some of them with next year’s monitoring due to the upward trend over the last three years (Table 7-1).

The aerial herbicide application would be applied on the entire 2,616 acres of the burned area. imazapic would be applied at a six ounce per acre rate and include appropriate adjuvants.
Actual_Implementation: Aerial Herbicide Application of imazapic on 2,617 acres was completed in October 2021 (FY22) with FY21 funds.\r\nThe proposed seeding areas are the focus of the aerial herbicide treatment of imazapic to prepare the seed bed for aerial seedings focusing on cheatgrass and noxious weed control for seedbed preparation for the aerial seeding treatment to enhance germination and seedling establishment of native perennials.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Treatment effectiveness plots were established during early summer 2022, allowing for monitoring during peak forb growth. Monitoring in 2022 showed, the invasive annual grass cover was 2.0% in the imazapic aerial herbicide area. The deep-rooted perennial grass total throughout the treatment was slightly over 8%. The shallow-rooted bunchgrasses have a total of 5.6% foliar cover in the 11.5% in the Imazapic treatment (Table 7-3, 7-4). Although the imazapic treatment has higher shallow-rooted bunchgrass cover, much of this cover is comprised of bulbous bluegrass (Poa bulbosa), a nonnative grass with little forage value following early spring. The imazapic plots overall had a density of 2.0 plants per m2 (Table 7-3). The imazapic area also showed higher species diversity of deep-rooted perennial grasses with five species of DRPGs compared to three DRPG species in the Telar and imazapic treated area.

Overall, in the two years since the Baldy fire, areas that received an aerial herbicide application of imazapic are recovering well with little invasive grass or forb presence. Imazapic treated area showed a high percentage of bare soil of 34% (Figure 7-4). These bare soil areas are traditionally thought to be highly susceptible to invasive annual grasses and will be important areas for monitoring in the future.

Monitoring in 2023 showed a moderate increase in invasive grass cover by a little over 8%, current invasive grass cover is 10.4% (Table 7-4). Deep-rooted perennial grass cover of had a similar increase or roughly 8%. Deep-rooted perennial grass now has a foliar cover of 15.8% within the treatment area. Currently, this area is not meeting any of the treatment objectives but looks like it might meet some of them with next year’s monitoring due to the upward trend over the last three years (Table 7-3).

Seed_Notes: Rate of application was approximately 5.0 pounds bulk seed per acre. The seed consisted of 3,300 pounds of Anatone Bluebunch Wheatgrass, 3,300 pounds of P-7 Bluebunch Wheatgrass, and 1,650 pounds of Sherman Big Bluegrass.
Objectives: The objective of the seeding treatment is to establish perennial-dominated plant communities within 3 years. The following grass density objectives are based on ecological site potential. The aerial seed treatments would be considered successful if: The seeded grass species reach densities of: \u2022 3 plants per square meter for grasses
Planned_Implementation: 1,646 acres of the burned acres are identified to be aerial seeded with a native perennial grass mix. The perennial grass mix is proposed to be accomplished in late fall FY21 prior to the chaining and mastication treatments. Although not all of the burn areas are being proposed for mastication and chaining, past ES & BAR monitoring data has shown that seeding steep slopes in phase 3 juniper without mastication or chaining can be highly successful in the re-establishment of seeded perennial grass species (2010 Emery Fire ES & BAR Monitoring Report).
Actual_Implementation: This project consisted of aerial seeding 1,647 acres of BLM land. This was an aerial grass seeding in the Conner Project Area, in the Burley Field Office. Rate of application was approximately 5.0 pounds bulk seed per acre. The seed consisted of 3,300 pounds of Anatone Bluebunch Wheatgrass, 3,300 pounds of P-7 Bluebunch Wheatgrass, and 1,650 pounds of Sherman Big Bluegrass. The seed was applied to bare muddy ground. The weather conditions were ideal with very little wind on the seeding day.\r\n\r\nThe contractor was High Desert Aviation, Inc of Gooding, ID.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY 22 Monitoring Results 
Quantitative data 
Aerial grass seeding 
Two years post-treatment the total density of aerially seeded grass species was 2.99 plants/m2 (Table 4), essentially meeting the treatment objective of 3 plants/m2. Bluebunch wheatgrass (Pseudoregeneria spicata) was the dominant seeded grass species in terms of density and cover, with Sherman’s big bluegrass (Poa secunda ‘sherman’) not recorded in 2022 (Tables 3-4). 
Cover and density of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) was higher in 2022 than in 2021, but still relatively low (Tables 3-4). Noxious weeds were not recorded on monitoring transects in either monitoring year (Tables 3-4). Other forbs accounted for most of the cover and density on Conner Summit monitoring plots in 2022, with an average of nearly 50% cover and 196.89 plants/m2 (Tables 3-4). Native annual forbs were abundant on all monitoring plots, with maiden blue-eyed Mary (Collinsia parviflora) and strict forget-me-not (Myosotis stricta) dominant species. Other grasses increased in cover in 2022, with an increase from 4.89 to 8.0 (Table 3), but density of other grasses decreased (Table 4). Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) was the dominant non-seeded perennial grass species, with squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) common, and basin wildrye (Leymus cinereus) frequent. Shrubs were an important component of recovering vegetation of the mountainous terrain of the Conner Summit ESR project area, with chokecherry (Prunus virginiana), common snowberry (Symphoricarpos albus), Saskatoon serviceberry (Amelanchier alnifolia), and yellow rabbitbrush (Chrysothamnus viscidiflorus), and wax current (Ribes cereum) among the species observed on monitoring plots. Noxious forbs were not recorded on monitoring transects. 
Cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) cover and density increased in 2022 relative to 2021 (Tables 3-4) and was considered common on 2 of the monitoring plots and rare on 1.

Summary 
Aerial grass 
Two years post-treatment, the Conner Summit ESR project area typically had very high native plant diversity, with native perennial grasses and forbs the dominant life forms. Seeded grass species essentially met treatment objectives by year 2 monitoring, with high cover and density of bluebunch wheatgrass. The mountainous terrain of the Conner Summit project area, with loamy soils, topographical diversity, and higher rainfall, supports productive, high diversity vegetation communities. Invasive plants were more abundant on lower elevation eastern slopes, where structural complexity of the recovering vegetation was lower.

The seed was applied to bare muddy ground on some areas and snow-covered ground in other areas. Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY 22 Monitoring Results 
Quantitative data 
Aerial sagebrush treatment 
Mountain big sagebrush was present at 0.0036 plants/m2 in both 2021 and 2022 (Table 5).
Qualitative Data 
Two years post-treatment the Conner Summit project area had excellent recovery of a perennial plant community with high native species diversity, structural complexity, and typically relatively low levels of invasive species. Native perennial forbs accounted for much of the species’ diversity observed on Conner Summit ESR monitoring plots, and native annual forbs such as maiden blue-eyed Mary were abundant. While noxious forbs were not recorded on the Conner Summit project transects, Canada thistle (Cirsium arvense) and Scotch thistle (Onopordum acanthium) were observed at low abundance on 1 plot. Invasive annual forbs were found on all plots, with species including tall tumblemustard (Sisymbrium altissimum), curveseed butterwort (Ceratocephala testiculata), littlepod false flax (Camelina microcarpa), prickly lettuce (Lactuca serriola), field pennycress (Thaspi arvense), and herb sophia (Descurainia sophia). Tall tumblemustard was abundant on 2 plots. The invasive perennial grass bulbous bluegrass (Poa bulbosa) was present on 1 plot. 
Monitoring photo points show significant increases in vegetative cover, vigor, and diversity from first- to second-year post-treatment monitoring (Figures 2-6). 
Mountain big sagebrush seedlings were observed on only 1 macroplot, where it was considered rare.
Summary 
Aerial sagebrush seeding treatments 
Aerial sagebrush seeding did not meet objectives for treatment success, with very low mountain big sagebrush density on belt transects, and mountain big sagebrush observed on only 1 monitoring plot. The windy and dry conditions of 2021 and winter 2022 likely impacted establishment of mountain big sagebrush, both due to a lack of moisture to support small seedlings, and a lack of moisture to support vegetation that could provide microsites for sagebrush establishment (Schuman and Belden 2002, Meyer and Warren 2015). Surviving patches of mountain big sagebrush were very rare within the fire area, so recruitment from survivors is unlikely to contribute to a return to a sagebrush dominated plant community.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The rehab objective of 0.3 native shrubs and 1 native forb per square meter has not been met for seeded species. No seeded species were observed within the density frames or species richness search of the plot. Most of the grass regrowth was composed of Sandbergs bluegrass although there were some observations of recovered Idaho fescue (Festuca idahoensis) and bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) made as well.
S3 Aerial Seeding
2020 AIM Data Results:
Cover: Average foliar canopy cover was moderately low (37.3%) with Sandbergs bluegrass (Poa secunda) at 16% cover and Idaho fescue (Festuca idahoensis) at 14% cover. Next highest foliar cover was derived from numerous perennial forbs such as longleaf phlox (Phlox longifolia), Hooker’s balsamroot (Balsamorhiza hookeri), and tapertip hawksbeard (Crepis accuminata) at 5.3%, 3.3%, and 2.7% cover, respectively. The only annual species captured in line-point intercept observations on the plot was tall annual willowherb (Epilobium brachycarpum) at 0.7% cover although field brome (Bromus arvensis) was observed in plot species inventory. Perennial grasses and forbs had a combined cover of 46.1% on the plots.
Gaps and Erosion
West Duck AIM Plot 01 is located in a Rangeland Claypan 12-16” P.Z. site in a former / Artemisia arbuscula / Festuca idahoensis – Pseudoroegneria spicata ( / low sagebrush / Idaho fescue - bluebunch wheatgrass) vegetation community on a linear fan piedmont. Soils were determined to be 3715 – Petan-Deunah-Hatpeak association (Deunah).
Approximately 47.9% of the transects had canopy gaps. The most frequently occurring gaps were 25-50 centimeters in length and these occupied 7 average meters (27.8%) of the 25 meter transects. No rills, gullies, or sheet erosion were observed on AIM Plot 01, although common pedestalling (with rare root exposure), rare deposition/runoff, and very short, rare water flow patterns were observed. These are a slight departure of expected conditions on the R025XY017NV site. The slope on AIM Plot 01 was estimated to be 6%, which is relatively low, indicating some wind or water erosion on the site.
Species Richness: A total of nineteen (19) different plants species were observed within the 2,827.4 square meter monitoring plot.
2020 Recommendations:
The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial seeding have not been fully met. There was no allotment agreement issued for the West Duck Fire area. However, typical agreement objective of three perennial grasses per square meter has been met (primarily through Sandbergs bluegrass). It is advised that the area receive appropriate rest and grazing management so that seeded species may establish.

2021 Density Results: 
2021: The rehab objective still has not been met for seeded species. Again, no seeded species were observed within the density frames or for species richness. Many of the same species dominate the plot as 2020, such as Sandberg’s bluegrass and Phlox species. Natural regrowth of small form bunchgrasses and forbs appear to be showing signs of recovery.
2021 AIM Data Results:
Average foliar canopy cover decreased to 28.00% from 37.3% last year. Perennial grasses dominate over the other indicators but are still only 20.67%. The next highest indicator is perennial forbs at 4.00%, which does mean that annuals are rare on the plot as well.
2021 Gaps and Erosion:
2021: The most frequently occurring gaps were 51-100cm at 30.01% with 25-50cm and 101-200cm nearly matching at 21.77% and 24.16% respectively. Although no data was collected on plot about signs of soil erosion, greater percentages of larger gaps could be an indicator of degrading soils. 
2021: Annual grasses and forbs were not observed during the species richness search but annual forbs were observed during Line-Point Intercept. Perennial species continued to outnumber annual species.
Recommendations 2021: 
The ESR rehabilitation objectives, as stated above in 2020 Recommendations, have not been fully met. Native regrowth meets the goals for grasses and forbs but no seeded species were observed on plot. It is still advised that the area receive appropriate rest, grazing management, and possibly more treatment to reach the goals for the site.

Objectives: The objective of the aerial seeding treatment is to revegetate the burned area with a well-adapted species mix that provides forage and will promote structural and species diversity within the burned area. Objectives will be considered met for the West Duck Aerial Sage Mix if 1 native forb and 0.3 native shrubs per square meter are found in post-fire monitoring within 2-5 years.
Planned_Implementation: Aerially seed approximately 4,452 acres of Wyoming big sagebrush, low sagebrush, and Western yarrow totaling 2,231 treated acres. The treatment would be completed in winter 2018/2019 after an application of imazapic. Timing of seeding would be coordinated with snowfall, if possible.
Actual_Implementation: Aerial PHMA Mix Applied: ACMIO, ARTRT, LIPE2, POSE, PSSPS, ARTRW8; Full coverage
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The rehab objective of 0.3 native shrubs and 1 native forb per square meter has not been met for seeded species. No seeded species were observed within the density frames or species richness search of the plot. Most of the grass regrowth was composed of Sandbergs bluegrass although there were some observations of recovered Idaho fescue (Festuca idahoensis) and bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) made as well.
S3 Aerial Seeding
2020 AIM Data Results:
Cover: Average foliar canopy cover was moderately low (37.3%) with Sandbergs bluegrass (Poa secunda) at 16% cover and Idaho fescue (Festuca idahoensis) at 14% cover. Next highest foliar cover was derived from numerous perennial forbs such as longleaf phlox (Phlox longifolia), Hooker’s balsamroot (Balsamorhiza hookeri), and tapertip hawksbeard (Crepis accuminata) at 5.3%, 3.3%, and 2.7% cover, respectively. The only annual species captured in line-point intercept observations on the plot was tall annual willowherb (Epilobium brachycarpum) at 0.7% cover although field brome (Bromus arvensis) was observed in plot species inventory. Perennial grasses and forbs had a combined cover of 46.1% on the plots.
Gaps and Erosion
West Duck AIM Plot 01 is located in a Rangeland Claypan 12-16” P.Z. site in a former / Artemisia arbuscula / Festuca idahoensis – Pseudoroegneria spicata ( / low sagebrush / Idaho fescue - bluebunch wheatgrass) vegetation community on a linear fan piedmont. Soils were determined to be 3715 – Petan-Deunah-Hatpeak association (Deunah).
Approximately 47.9% of the transects had canopy gaps. The most frequently occurring gaps were 25-50 centimeters in length and these occupied 7 average meters (27.8%) of the 25 meter transects. No rills, gullies, or sheet erosion were observed on AIM Plot 01, although common pedestalling (with rare root exposure), rare deposition/runoff, and very short, rare water flow patterns were observed. These are a slight departure of expected conditions on the R025XY017NV site. The slope on AIM Plot 01 was estimated to be 6%, which is relatively low, indicating some wind or water erosion on the site.
Species Richness: A total of nineteen (19) different plants species were observed within the 2,827.4 square meter monitoring plot.
2020 Recommendations:
The ESR rehabilitation objectives of the aerial seeding have not been fully met. There was no allotment agreement issued for the West Duck Fire area. However, typical agreement objective of three perennial grasses per square meter has been met (primarily through Sandbergs bluegrass). It is advised that the area receive appropriate rest and grazing management so that seeded species may establish.

2021 Density Results: 
2021: The rehab objective still has not been met for seeded species. Again, no seeded species were observed within the density frames or for species richness. Many of the same species dominate the plot as 2020, such as Sandberg’s bluegrass and Phlox species. Natural regrowth of small form bunchgrasses and forbs appear to be showing signs of recovery.
2021 AIM Data Results:
Average foliar canopy cover decreased to 28.00% from 37.3% last year. Perennial grasses dominate over the other indicators but are still only 20.67%. The next highest indicator is perennial forbs at 4.00%, which does mean that annuals are rare on the plot as well.
2021 Gaps and Erosion:
2021: The most frequently occurring gaps were 51-100cm at 30.01% with 25-50cm and 101-200cm nearly matching at 21.77% and 24.16% respectively. Although no data was collected on plot about signs of soil erosion, greater percentages of larger gaps could be an indicator of degrading soils. 
2021: Annual grasses and forbs were not observed during the species richness search but annual forbs were observed during Line-Point Intercept. Perennial species continued to outnumber annual species.
Recommendations 2021: 
The ESR rehabilitation objectives, as stated above in 2020 Recommendations, have not been fully met. Native regrowth meets the goals for grasses and forbs but no seeded species were observed on plot. It is still advised that the area receive appropriate rest, grazing management, and possibly more treatment to reach the goals for the site.

Objectives: To protect the burned areas from unauthorized livestock use in order to help ensure vegetation recovery.
Planned_Implementation: To ensure that the agreement is written and presented to the permittee.
Actual_Implementation: A handful of sites were reviewed by an Interdisciplinary Team to evaluate reintroduction of grazing to those select pastures.  Cover, seedhead production counts, and grass pulls to test rooting strength were used to evaluate the recovery of these sites and to help determine if they could withstand grazing.  The results were written into memos outlining the criteria for reintroduction of grazing, and the terms to be held up while grazing occurs, such as duration, timing, and utilization percentages.  The East 71 Pasture of Grassy Hills AMP Allotment and Turner Cedar Butte Allotment have met the criteria established post Murphy Fire and are scheduled to be reopened in the fall of 2008.  Other sites have been identified for review in late August and early September, and are being analyzed currently.  If the criteria for reopening are met, then the pastures will be open during their normal seasons of use.  In 2009, all of the sites will have the grazing reintroduction monitoring performed in addition to the normal monitoring procedures, unless grazing has been implemented at that site prior to the second year of monitoring.\r\n\r\nThe Natural Recovery sites which were rested to livestock grazing in order to aid in recovery area recovering as expected in the first year following a fire.  Four areas have been identified as needing treatment in the form of herbicide control for cheatgrass and seeding the appropriate seed mix for the site.  These sites will be monitored as seeding treatments following treatment.  Erosion is an issue at some sites, but appears to be minimizing.  Further monitoring is needed to determine if a trend towards natural recovery is being made.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: Effectiveness monitoring will include visits to the site by range staff and other BLM employees to ensure that there is no livestock within the burned area and that no unauthorized use has taken place.
